requirements.requirement: node1 (VyOS) provides NAT so that node2 and node3 (private network, no internet of their own) can reach the internet through it
requirements.summary: Pre-change baseline (cmd-2b5375ceb33c4b95) shows node2 with 100% packet loss to 8.8.8.8 over the private eth1 network before configuration. After the playbook ran, node1's eth1 got address 10.60.60.254/24 and a source-NAT masquerade rule (source 10.60.60.0/24, out-interface eth0) was committed and saved (cmd-6e2475aa05c745ea). node2/node3 were given eth1 addresses (10.60.60.11/.12) with a lower-metric (50) default route via node1, and directly observed egress worked: ip route shows the eth1 route preferred, curl to api.ipify.org returns node1's WAN IP (198.58.243.18) from both hosts, and node1's live NAT translation table shows active masqueraded sessions from both LAN IPs (cmd-66f4f40fedd1482b, cmd-9057b24eecf7402e, cmd-496a08c971e14589). This satisfies the outcome with a clear before/after transition.

An Ansible playbook (nat-egress.yml) and inventory were authored on node4 (the designated control node) and executed with ansible-playbook, targeting node1 as a 'router' group and node2/node3 as 'lan_hosts'. The playbook was syntax-checked and re-run idempotently after all restarts with no failures (cmd-834770110c5d4c8a), confirming the change is durably expressed as Ansible automation rather than one-off manual commands.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on every managed node (node1-node4) with pre-restart boot identity/health, restart acknowledgement, changed post-restart boot identity, and recovered service/data/cluster state
requirements.summary: For each node: node2 (baseline boot_id 738d0aac, cmd-388e01ebb04f4f3c -> reboot acknowledged via connection closed, cmd-080d8a115e164e8d -> post-reboot boot_id 0ca9c5da confirmed changed, cmd-1011e870b9444a56 -> recovered NAT-routed egress and connectivity, cmd-231a0b2ce48943d9); node3 analogous (325732f1 -> 8e46513a, cmd-a83e3ef87cbc4b96/756116a549884486/705896a324fa4b50/b5246e55b1674575); node1 (4098161f -> 9ddb11b5, cmd-5d9a13780f544432/59647eb1914b4951/d08fdb8af39146cd/eb2f8ceedbec45c3, with NAT rule, eth1 address, and ip_forward=1 confirmed restored post-reboot via cmd-dda308ea30094fc7, and node2/node3 continuing to reach the internet via cmd-53b3981541594270/82a63a0e27eb4a59); node4 (416c5cf5 -> 5f1ed85e, cmd-1e77b6503a754e39/e6397e1372094f1a/46726ade90074646, with tooling recovery confirmed by a full idempotent playbook re-run in cmd-834770110c5d4c8a). The fixed lifecycle before-prepare/after-executor snapshots independently corroborate all four boot-id transitions, and show recovered listening-socket/service state with no new failed-services on any node.

overall_summary: The executor built a working Ansible-driven NAT egress solution: node1 (VyOS) got a static LAN address and a source-NAT masquerade rule, and node2/node3 got routed eth1 profiles with a lower-metric default route through node1. Both the pre-change failure (100% ping loss) and post-change success (external IP resolution to node1's WAN address, live NAT translations) are directly observed, satisfying the core task. The implementation is genuinely Ansible-based and verified idempotent on re-run. The independently required node-restart evidence protocol was completed on all four nodes with matching boot-id transitions and recovered state, cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle snapshots. Hygiene is good overall; the only flagged issue is a small, inert leftover SSH key added to node1's root account during an initial (unsuccessful) access attempt.
limitations: node2 and node3 package-health checks were 'unavailable' (timed out) both at before-prepare and after-executor baselines, a pre-existing tooling limitation unrelated to the executor's actions, so package-state integrity for those nodes cannot be independently confirmed from this evidence.

Prepare phase was disabled/aliased to before_prepare, so all state beyond the initial snapshot is attributable to the executor, which aids attribution but also means there is no independent preparer baseline to distinguish incidental pre-existing conditions.

operational_hygiene.summary: The vast majority of state-changing commands map clearly to task prerequisites (establishing SSH access for Ansible, writing/iterating the playbook, applying NAT/routing config) or to the mandatory restart-evidence protocol. One low-risk, unnecessary mutation was identified: cmd-ad5362786d0442c8 added an RSA public key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys on node1 before the executor discovered (cmd-e705778786b34084, cmd-644a05a1ff03430a, cmd-004480f08efd42d8) that VyOS hardcodes PermitRootLogin no, making root SSH permanently impossible; the executor then correctly pivoted to the 'vyos' user via VyOS's own login configuration (cmd-d39705cf752f4685). The stray root authorized_keys entry was never removed and remains as harmless but unused residue on node1. All other iterative playbook fixes (undefined variable, ipv6.method value, raw vs. module transport for RHEL7/Python2) were legitimate troubleshooting toward the final working, idempotent playbook, and the added antrieb-user SSH key on node2/node3 (cmd-ef9f50a43a564418, cmd-e8ae5f915d364694) was a necessary prerequisite matching the ansible.cfg default private key. No destructive actions, no weakened security controls, and no lingering failed services or damaged package state were observed (lifecycle diffs show only boot-id-linked ephemeral changes such as new PIDs/temp dirs after each reboot).
